channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: Digital Therapeutic Interventions for Suicide Prevention: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Their Effectiveness in Reducing Suicidal Ideation and Suicide Attempts.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study addresses whether digital therapeutic interventions (e.g., apps, online programs) reduce suicidal ideation or suicide attempts in randomized clinical trials (RCTs). It synthesizes 17 RCTs (N = 5,089) to clarify mixed prior findings and assess durability of effects.
FINDINGS: Digital interventions significantly reduced suicidal ideation immediately (Hedges’ g = –0.61, 95 % CI not reported) and at follow-up (g = –0.77). The relative risk of suicide attempts was reduced (RR ≈ 0.7–0.8) but not statistically significant. Effects were larger in clinical populations, self-guided formats, and younger participants; heterogeneity was high (I² not reported).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate-sized but heterogeneous, with potential risk of bias across diverse digital formats and control conditions. The statistically significant reduction in suicidal ideation is of uncertain clinical magnitude; the non-significant trend for fewer attempts precludes firm conclusions. Publication bias assessment was limited and funding sources were not disclosed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Digital interventions may offer a useful adjunct for reducing suicidal thoughts, especially in younger or clinical subgroups, but current evidence does not yet justify replacing standard care for suicide prevention. Clinicians should monitor emerging high-quality RCTs before integrating these tools routinely.

item.title: Periodized Resistance Training Versus Aerobic Training in Managing Nonspecific Chronic Low Back Pain: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study is a randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing periodized resistance training (RT) versus aerobic training (AT) for managing nonspecific chronic low back pain (NSCLBP), focusing on pain, disability, kinesiophobia, and physical performance. The population consists of 38 adults with NSCLBP, randomized to RT (n=19) or AT (n=19).
FINDINGS: All 38 participants completed the 8-week intervention. RT showed significantly lower adjusted post-treatment scores for pain (AMD = -2.71, 95% CI -3.17 to -2.25, p < 0.001), disability (AMD = -0.20, 95% CI -0.25 to -0.15, p < 0.001), and kinesiophobia (AMD = -5.54, 95% CI -7.89 to -3.19, p < 0.001). RT also improved strength and endurance measures with large effect sizes (η²p = 0.480–0.804).
INTERPRETATION: The study has high internal validity due to randomization, ANCOVA adjustment for baseline imbalances, and complete follow-up. However, the small sample size (n=38) and short duration (8 weeks) limit generalizability and long-term conclusions. The large effect sizes suggest clinical relevance, but replication in larger, longer trials is needed to confirm durability and broader applicability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Periodized resistance training may be a more effective rehabilitation option than aerobic training for NSCLBP in the short term, particularly for reducing pain, disability, and kinesiophobia. Clinicians may consider RT for patients with NSCLBP, but should monitor long-term outcomes and individual tolerance.

item.title: Learning from neurodivergent students about their mental health and wellbeing during transition to secondary school: A systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study addresses how the transition from primary to secondary school affects mental health and wellbeing in neurodivergent children (e.g., autistic youth, those with developmental language disorder, or Down syndrome), using a neurodiversity-informed framework. It is a systematic review of longitudinal empirical studies with child-reported outcomes, aiming to clarify inconsistent findings in this emerging research area.
FINDINGS: Out of 488 records screened, only 10 studies met inclusion criteria, all longitudinal with comparison groups and at least two timepoints around the school transition. Due to substantial heterogeneity, a narrative synthesis was conducted. Findings on mental health outcomes were mixed and inconclusive, but psychosocial factors—such as school belonging and connectedness—showed more consistent vulnerability signals. Key gaps included lack of participatory research, underrepresentation of certain neurodivergent groups, and limited attention to intersectional factors like ethnicity and socioeconomic status.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is very limited and heterogeneous, with no meta-analysis possible. The reliance on narrative synthesis and small, varied samples reduces confidence in any firm conclusions. The stronger signal in psychosocial outcomes suggests these may be more sensitive indicators than mental health symptoms, but causality and clinical significance remain unclear. The absence of co-produced research and intersectional analyses limits generalisability and clinical applicability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not support specific clinical recommendations for managing mental health during school transition in neurodivergent youth. Clinicians should prioritise monitoring psychosocial adjustment (e.g., belonging, school concerns) rather than assuming uniform mental health deterioration. Future practice should await more rigorous, participatory, and intersectionally informed research before implementing targeted interventions.

item.title: Depression and reward function in adolescence and the potential of behavioral activation as a treatment: a narrative review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines whether reward function is a key mechanism in adolescent depression and whether Behavioral Activation (BA), a reward-focused therapy, is effective and feasible for adolescents. It synthesizes cross-disciplinary evidence to address gaps in current treatments and the mechanisms underlying adolescent depression.
FINDINGS: The review reports that BA shows promise as an effective and feasible treatment for adolescent depression, aligning with calls from NICE for further research. However, the mechanisms by which BA works in adolescence remain unclear, and there are unresolved questions about its optimal delivery. The evidence base is described as underpowered, with tensions across neuroscience, psychology, and clinical practice.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this study lacks the methodological rigor of systematic reviews or randomized trials, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about BA’s efficacy or the role of reward function in adolescent depression. The lack of quantitative data (e.g., effect sizes, confidence intervals) limits the ability to assess the strength of the evidence. The review highlights important gaps but does not resolve them, underscoring the need for high-quality trials to clarify mechanisms and optimize BA delivery.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: BA may be a viable treatment option for adolescent depression, but current evidence is insufficient to recommend it over established treatments. Clinicians should remain cautious and consider BA as an adjunct or experimental approach while awaiting more robust evidence. Further research is needed to determine its place in routine care.

item.title: Metabolic syndrome in stable long-term antipsychotic monotherapy and polypharmacy among patients with schizophrenia: a real-world comparative study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This retrospective cohort study in a Swedish community mental health centre asked whether antipsychotic polypharmacy, compared with monotherapy, is independently associated with metabolic syndrome in adults with schizophrenia who had been on a stable regimen for ≥5 years. 370 patients were included.
FINDINGS: Metabolic syndrome was present in 38.6 % overall (41.2 % polypharmacy vs 34.7 % monotherapy, p = 0.216). Polypharmacy patients had higher chlorpromazine-equivalent doses (median 1010 vs 454.5 mg/day, p < 0.001) and more LAI use (67.3 % vs 37.5 %, p < 0.001). In multivariable logistic regression, neither polypharmacy (adjusted OR 1.220, 95 % CI 0.767–1.941, p = 0.401), daily dose increments of 100 mg (adjusted OR 1.003, 95 % CI 0.954–1.055, p = 0.899), nor LAI use were independently linked to metabolic syndrome. Current smoking showed the only independent association (adjusted OR 1.996, 95 % CI 1.251–3.185, p = 0.004).
INTERPRETATION: The study’s retrospective design and selection of long-term stable patients limit causal inference; residual confounding (e.g., illness severity, prior treatments) cannot be excluded. The confidence intervals around the null associations are wide, so clinically meaningful effects cannot be ruled out. The clearest modifiable risk factor was smoking, underscoring the need for cardiometabolic monitoring and smoking cessation interventions regardless of regimen.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For patients on long-term antipsychotic treatment, switching from polypharmacy to monotherapy primarily to reduce metabolic risk is not supported by these data. Focus should remain on routine metabolic screening and smoking cessation rather than regimen simplification per se.

item.title: Peripartum Esketamine: A Narrative Review of Analgesia, Postpartum Depressive Symptoms, Sleep-Related Outcomes, and Safety.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines whether peripartum esketamine can improve pain control, reduce postpartum depressive symptoms, enhance sleep, and maintain maternal-infant safety. It synthesizes mechanistic rationale and clinical studies, primarily single-center trials in cesarean-delivery populations.
FINDINGS: Short-term analgesic benefit is consistently reported, but opioid-sparing effects are inconsistent. Several RCTs suggest low-dose peri-delivery esketamine may lower early Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) screening positives, though diagnostic outcomes are sparse. Sleep benefits are preliminary and based on subjective measures. Maternal and neonatal tolerability appear acceptable in the short term, but pregnancy pharmacokinetics, lactation data, and long-term offspring neurodevelopment remain insufficiently studied.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by study design heterogeneity, small single-center samples, and reliance on screening tools rather than diagnostic interviews. Strengths include consistent short-term analgesic findings and signals for mood improvement, but the lack of objective sleep measures, standardized dosing, and long-term safety data constrains confidence. The clinical significance of observed mood effects is uncertain given the absence of diagnostic confirmation and long-term follow-up.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Esketamine may be considered as an individualized adjunct for peripartum pain management, but routine prophylactic use for mood or sleep is not supported by current evidence. Clinicians should await larger multicenter trials with diagnostic outcomes and long-term safety assessments before changing practice.

item.title: Feasibility and Acceptability of Videoconference-Based Family Psychoeducation for Young Adult Caregivers of Family Members With Major Depressive Disorder: Protocol for a Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a protocol for a waitlist-controlled pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT) examining the feasibility and acceptability of videoconference-based family psychoeducation (vFPE) for young adult caregivers (aged 18–39) of family members with major depressive disorder (MDD). The study addresses a gap in support programs for this vulnerable group, who face psychological distress and caregiving burdens during a critical developmental period.
FINDINGS: The protocol outlines a 1:1 randomized trial with 4 weekly 40-minute vFPE sessions. Primary outcomes are feasibility (recruitment, randomization, completion, dropout, safety) and acceptability (Client Satisfaction Questionnaire-8). Exploratory outcomes (e.g., anxiety, depression, caregiver burden) will be assessed at baseline, postintervention, and 1-month follow-up. As of May 2026, 8 participants had been enrolled, with recruitment and data collection ongoing until March 2028.
INTERPRETATION: This is a feasibility study, not designed to test efficacy. Strengths include its randomized design and focus on a neglected population, but conclusions are premature given the small sample size and ongoing recruitment. The protocol’s rigor depends on adherence to randomization and blinding (if any), but no effect sizes or preliminary results are yet available. External validity is uncertain until feasibility metrics (e.g., dropout rates, satisfaction) are reported.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No clinical conclusions can be drawn yet. If feasibility is demonstrated, this could pave the way for a larger RCT to assess effectiveness. Clinicians should monitor future results to determine whether vFPE is a viable option for young adult caregivers in routine care.

item.title: The science of child and adolescent mental health in Mozambique: A systematic review of prevalence estimates, measurement tools, and interventions.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Mozambique has a large population of children and adolescents with limited mental health research representation. This systematic review synthesizes evidence on prevalence estimates, measurement tools, and interventions for mental health outcomes in individuals aged 0–19 years in Mozambique, addressing a critical gap in underrepresented populations.
FINDINGS: The review identified 81 publications: 61 reports with prevalence data from 25 studies, 29 reports on 42 assessment instruments, and 9 intervention reports (including 8 trials). Two clinical surveys reported prevalence estimates: ADHD 13.4% (N=748, 6–18 years) in Nampula and any mental disorder 23% (with anxiety 17.5%, major depression 8.5%, disruptive behavior 6.6%, substance use 4.5%, ADHD 3.3%, PTSD 1.2%; N=486, 12–19 years) in Maputo. Nationally representative adolescent surveys showed high exposure to violence (e.g., 24.86% annual physical/emotional violence). Only four instruments (MINI-KID, GAD-7, PHQ-A, SDQ) were cross-culturally adapted with reliable psychometrics. One RCT reported a cost-effective neurodevelopmental intervention for high-poverty preschoolers.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited, heterogeneous, and geographically concentrated, with only two clinical prevalence surveys and one RCT. Psychometric validity of tools is uncertain unless adapted, and high adversity exposure suggests a substantial unmet need. The single RCT provides preliminary support for early intervention but cannot be generalized without replication. Funding sources and risk of bias were not reported, limiting confidence in the findings. More rigorous, representative studies with culturally validated tools are urgently needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice in Mozambique is constrained by a lack of validated assessment tools and limited intervention evidence. Clinicians should use adapted instruments (e.g., MINI-KID, SDQ) where available and consider early developmental interventions in high-risk settings, while recognizing the paucity of robust local data to guide decisions.

item.title: [Expert Council resolution: adjunctive pharmacotherapy for hyperkinetic disorders (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) in children and adolescents].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The Expert Council of the National Association of Pediatric Neurologists in Russia reviewed adjunctive pharmacotherapy options for ADHD in children and adolescents, focusing on medications beyond international first-line standards. This expert consensus (not a systematic review or RCT) stratified medications into two groups based on evidence strength using the 2019 CECCMP system.
FINDINGS: Group A (strongest evidence) includes Prospekta, supported by double-blind RCTs achieving primary ADHD endpoints. Group B (limited evidence) includes Cortexin, Tenoten for children, Cerebrolysin, Semax, Cogitum, Magne B6, Pantoham, and Mexidol. Adjunctive pharmacotherapy is recommended only as part of a multidisciplinary approach (psychoeducation + behavioral interventions) and not as a substitute for atomoxetine in eligible patients.
INTERPRETATION: This is an expert consensus statement with inherent limitations: no systematic literature review, no quantitative effect sizes, and no direct comparison to standard treatments. The evidence grading relies on the CECCMP system, which may not align with international standards. The clinical applicability of Group B medications remains uncertain due to lack of robust evidence. The recommendation to avoid substituting atomoxetine is pragmatic but not evidence-based in this summary.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For now, this resolution does not change clinical practice outside Russia. Standard first-line ADHD treatments (e.g., atomoxetine, methylphenidate) remain the basis of care. Clinicians should await higher-quality evidence before considering adjunctive agents listed in Group B.

item.title: Parental beliefs, initiation of alcohol consumption, and binge drinking among Brazilian adolescents.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study nested within a cluster RCT examined whether parental beliefs about adolescent alcohol use are associated with initiation of drinking and binge drinking among 859 Brazilian adolescents aged 10–14 years.
FINDINGS: Parents who believed it was safer to teach children to drink at home had twice the odds of adolescent alcohol initiation (OR 2.10, 95 % CI not reported). The belief that “drinking only at parties is harmless” was associated with a 2.61-fold increase in odds of binge drinking. Harmful parental alcohol use or probable dependence increased adolescent alcohol consumption eightfold (OR 8.00, 95 % CI not reported).
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests permissive parental beliefs and parental alcohol misuse correlate with higher adolescent alcohol use, but as a cross-sectional analysis it cannot prove causality. Key limitations include lack of confidence intervals, potential self-report bias, and no adjustment for peer or school-level factors. The large OR for parental misuse is striking but should be interpreted cautiously until replicated in longitudinal designs.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings support screening parents’ attitudes and alcohol use when assessing adolescent drinking risk, but do not yet justify changing primary prevention strategies beyond current evidence-based family interventions.

item.title: A Typology of Moderator Practices and Community Guidelines in Online Mental Health Communities to Establish a Framework for Digital Safety: Systematized Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Online mental health communities (OMHCs) provide peer support but face challenges in ensuring safety and supportive interactions through moderation practices and community guidelines. This systematized review aimed to develop typologies of moderator practices and guideline content in OMHCs for people with mental health problems, synthesizing empirical and gray literature from 2014 to 2024.
FINDINGS: The review included 80 documents (48 empirical papers and 32 gray literature) covering 52 OMHCs. Four categories of moderator practices were identified: (1) premoderation/postmoderation processes (used in 79% of OMHCs), (2) reactive moderation, (3) community-building, and (4) member monitoring. Three categories of community guideline content emerged: (1) content of posts (used in 67% of OMHCs), (2) member conduct, and (3) moderation. Thematic analysis synthesized these findings into a structured framework.
INTERPRETATION: This systematized review provides a structured framework for moderator practices and guideline content in OMHCs, addressing a critical gap in digital safety. Strengths include the broad inclusion of empirical and gray literature and the development of actionable typologies. However, as a systematized review (not a full systematic review), it lacks formal risk-of-bias assessment and may overrepresent certain OMHCs. The findings are descriptive and lack quantitative effect sizes or comparative data. External validity depends on the diversity of OMHCs included, which may not fully represent all platforms or cultural contexts.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This framework could guide the development of moderator training, digital tools, and governance policies in OMHCs, potentially improving safety and support for users. Clinicians should be aware of these typologies when recommending or evaluating OMHCs, but further research is needed to assess their impact on user outcomes and safety.

item.title: Altered GABAB receptor sensitivity in heavy drinkers indexed using a TMS-based biomarker: a randomized controlled experimental medicine trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study tested whether heavy alcohol use alters sensitivity of metabotropic GABAB receptors (GABABRs) using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) biomarkers and a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design in 31 healthy volunteers (16 heavy drinkers, 15 light drinkers).
FINDINGS: Baclofen 30 mg and 60 mg produced dose-dependent increases in growth hormone (GH) release, confirming central GABABR engagement. Long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI) increased after baclofen in light drinkers at both doses, suggesting a plateau effect. In heavy drinkers, LICI increased at 30 mg but not at 60 mg despite similar drug levels, indicating altered GABABR sensitivity under higher agonist stimulation.
INTERPRETATION: The randomized crossover design and biomarker confirmation strengthen internal validity. The small sample and healthy volunteer population limit generalizability to clinical AUD. The differential LICI response at higher dose suggests altered receptor function in heavy drinkers, but clinical significance remains uncertain without outcome data.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Findings support further investigation of TMS-based biomarkers for GABABR target engagement but do not yet justify changes in AUD treatment. Watch for emerging studies linking these biomarkers to clinical outcomes.

item.title: Exercise as a complementary intervention for adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a neurobiological analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review explores potential neurobiological mechanisms by which physical exercise could alleviate symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity in adults with ADHD, where evidence for exercise as a treatment is limited compared to children.
FINDINGS: The review synthesizes mechanistic hypotheses—including enhanced neuroplasticity, improved functional brain connectivity, neurotransmitter modulation, and reduced neuroinflammation—based on heterogeneous, largely observational data and indirect evidence from non-ADHD populations. No clinical outcome data or effect sizes are reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and methodologically weak: reliance on a single database, single-author screening, and lack of direct adult ADHD intervention studies limit internal validity. The proposed mechanisms are biologically plausible but remain unconfirmed in the target population. External validity is uncertain due to indirect data sources.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Exercise may hold promise as a low-cost, accessible adjunct for adults with ADHD, but current evidence is insufficient to recommend it as a treatment. Clinicians should view exercise as supportive care while awaiting rigorous trials to confirm efficacy and clarify mechanisms.

item.title: Design, reporting, and research focus of neurology and psychiatry drug trials (2020-2023): a registry-based meta-epidemiological study using ClinicalTrials.gov and NLP.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This registry-based meta-epidemiological study used ClinicalTrials.gov data (2000–2023) with NLP and manual validation to quantify design features, reporting practices, and research focus in neurology and psychiatry drug trials. The clinical question concerns how these trials are conducted and reported, which affects evidence synthesis and future trial planning.
FINDINGS: Among 18,609 trials, most were early-phase (60% completed), single-center, and small (median 11–50 participants). Industry funded 36%, declining over time; university sponsorship increased. Ten percent were non-randomized and 38% open-label. Among trials completed after 2007, only 50% reported results, with a mean delay of 12 months. Top conditions studied were pain (10%), schizophrenia (8%), depression (8%), and Alzheimer’s disease (7%). Atypical antipsychotics, levodopa, and ketamine each accounted for 1–2% of trials.
INTERPRETATION: The study highlights persistent deficiencies in trial design (small size, high proportion of non-randomized/open-label trials) and poor results reporting (only half reported results, often delayed). While the large sample size and use of NLP strengthen internal validity, reliance on registry data and lack of clinical outcome assessment limit external validity. The findings suggest a need for improved adherence to reporting standards and better trial design to enhance evidence quality.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should be cautious when interpreting underpowered, open-label, or industry-funded trials in neurology and psychiatry. Improved trial registration and results reporting are essential for evidence-based practice.

item.title: Twelve-month follow-up of parent-based child anxiety treatment.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether gains from Supportive Parenting for Anxious Childhood Emotions (SPACE), a parent-based treatment for child anxiety, are maintained up to 12 months post-treatment compared to cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). It was a 12-month follow-up of a randomized controlled noninferiority trial involving 125 mother-child dyads.
FINDINGS: Both SPACE and CBT led to significant reductions in child anxiety severity and family accommodation over time, with gains maintained similarly through 12 months. Parent-reported child anxiety severity was lower for SPACE than CBT at posttreatment and 12-month follow-up (effect sizes not specified in the abstract). No comparative data were provided for child-reported anxiety severity at follow-up.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides moderate-quality evidence that SPACE and CBT maintain treatment gains over 12 months, with a potential advantage for SPACE in parent-reported outcomes. However, the lack of effect sizes, confidence intervals, and blinding raises concerns about bias and precision. The reliance on parent reports and absence of child-reported differences at follow-up limit conclusions about clinical meaningfulness. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and explore mechanisms of change.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: SPACE may be a viable alternative to CBT for child anxiety, particularly when parental involvement is desired or CBT access is limited. Clinicians should consider parent preferences and monitor outcomes using both parent and child reports to guide treatment decisions.

item.title: Extended reality as an assistive technology for mental health and wellbeing: a scoping review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review asks whether Extended Reality (XR—virtual, augmented, and mixed reality) can meaningfully advance mental-health care across conditions such as anxiety, depression, PTSD, ADHD, and autism, given persistent barriers to conventional treatments. Using PRISMA-ScR methods, 277 empirical studies published January 2022–March 2025 were synthesised thematically.
FINDINGS: XR applications spanned anxiety/stress (most frequently studied), depression/mood disorders, PTSD, neurodevelopmental conditions, social isolation, cognitive decline, and workplace stress. Reported benefits were predominantly short-term or preliminary, especially for anxiety and PTSD. Design approaches included immersive exposure, mindfulness/relaxation, social interaction, cognitive stimulation, biofeedback, haptics, and adaptive personalisation. Key constraints were limited longitudinal and comparative evidence, high costs, accessibility barriers, clinician training needs, and ethical/privacy/regulatory concerns.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and heterogeneous; most studies are small, short-term, and lack robust comparators. While XR shows promise—particularly for anxiety and PTSD—there is insufficient high-quality evidence to establish sustained clinical impact or cost-effectiveness. Stronger randomised trials with longer follow-up, pragmatic comparisons to usual care, and attention to equity, training, and regulation are needed before widespread adoption.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, XR should be considered experimental for routine psychiatric care; clinicians may cautiously explore XR tools in anxiety/PTSD within research or highly supervised settings, but should not yet adopt them as standard interventions.

item.title: Suicidal Ideation and Influencing Factors in Adolescents With Non-Suicidal Self-Injury.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional, multicenter study in central China investigated the prevalence and correlates of suicidal ideation among 3730 adolescents with non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), addressing a gap in population-level evidence for school-based mental health initiatives.
FINDINGS: Among the 3730 adolescents with NSSI, 74.05% reported past-year suicidal ideation, and 68.2% were classified as high suicide risk. Multiple linear regression identified female sex, only-child status, higher parental education, greater depressive and anxiety symptoms, and poorer family functioning as significant correlates of higher suicidal ideation (p < 0.05).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides robust population-level data from a large sample, but its cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. Reliance on self-report measures and single-region sampling limits generalizability to other settings. While the associations are statistically significant, their clinical magnitude and causal pathways remain unclear without longitudinal or interventional validation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The findings support routine screening for suicidal ideation in adolescents with NSSI, particularly in school settings, and highlight the need to assess mood symptoms and family functioning. However, the high prevalence underscores the urgency of intervention rather than introducing new practices.

item.title: An Automated Framework Using Magnetic Resonance Imaging Feature Masking and Support Vector Machine for Schizophrenia Classification.
item.description: Automated classification of schizophrenia can improve the quality of life for people with schizophrenia and reduce social costs. At present, however, the usual standards for diagnosing mental illnesses are still based on the subjective assessment of psychiatrists and lack objective quantitative biomarkers for early detection. Neuroimaging-based machine learning has achieved some success, but the existing models have not addressed the high dimensionality of small-sample magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies.

item.title: Fatty Acid Supplementation in Toddlers Born Preterm and Attention and Autism Outcomes at 8-10 Years: Omega Tots Randomized Controlled Trial Long-Term Follow-Up.
item.description: PURPOSE: Children born preterm are at increased likelihood of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). We examined whether 6 months of daily dietary docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) + arachidonic acid (AA) supplementation at age 1-year reduced attention problems and likelihood of ADHD and ASD diagnoses in children born preterm. METHODS: In the Omega Tots randomized placebo-controlled trial, children born at <35 weeks' gestation received daily DHA (200 mg) + AA (200 mg) or placebo (400 mg corn oil) at 10-16 months' corrected age.

item.title: Opposing Patterns of the Histone Variant MacroH2A1.1 in Fmr1 Knockout and BTBR T+ Itpr3tf/J Mouse Models of Autism Spectrum Disorder.
item.description: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) exhibits substantial heterogeneity, wherein genetic and idiopathic forms may converge on shared core phenotypes through divergent molecular pathways. The histone variant macroH2A1.1, implicated in chromatin repression and DNA repair, has been linked to behavioral alterations opposite to core ASD features when depleted systemically. However, its regional and cell-type-specific regulation in genetic versus idiopathic ASD models remains unclear.

item.title: Adult Adhd Knowledge, Practices and Training Needs Among Psychiatrists in Tuscany. Results from the Auto-Sag Survey.
item.description: OBJECTIVE: the clinical management of adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in Italy takes place without consolidated national guidelines and within a regulatory framework originally designed for paediatric populations. This study aimed to describe psychiatrists' knowledge, diagnostic and therapeutic practices, regulatory awareness, and training needs regarding adult ADHD, and to test whether specific ADHD training, rather than general clinical experience, predicted perceived preparedness.

item.title: Prenatal psychological care to prevent emotional and reproductive complications in pregnancy after perinatal loss: a mixed methods study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: The loss of a child in the perinatal period can have devastating psychological, physical, and social impacts, which can extend to subsequent pregnancies and parenting. The present study aimed to understand women's perceptions of the factors involved in pregnancy following perinatal loss and to analyze the results of the "Psychological Prenatal" psychotherapeutic intervention developed with the aim of reducing emotional distress and adverse obstetric outcomes.

item.title: Positive-affective and negative-cognitive brain-behavior axes in clinical high risk for psychosis.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR) present with heterogeneous combinations of positive, negative, and affective symptoms, cognitive difficulties, and functional impairment. However, reproducible multivariate links between this multidomain phenotype and brain morphology remain limited. This study explored the multivariate brain-behavior associations in CHR using a data-driven approach.

item.title: Inherited and early-life vulnerability in functional neurological disorder and functional somatic symptoms: A retrospective cohort and case-control study from a large electronic health record database.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Biological factors affecting motor, sensory, and integrative processing may predispose to functional neurological disorder (FND) and functional somatic symptoms. While early-life influences have traditionally been conceptualized within psychological frameworks, the contribution of early-life biological vulnerabilities to symptom expression remains unclear. METHODS: Using TriNetX, a large electronic health records database, we assessed proportions of inherited, congenital, perinatal, and neurodevelopmental diagnoses, capturing a range of early-life conditions.

item.title: Effects of childhood maltreatment on emotional intelligence and psychosocial functioning in adult euthymic bipolar disorder patients compared with healthy controls.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Childhood maltreatment (CM) has been linked to poor emotional intelligence (EI) and psychosocial functioning (PSF) in patients with bipolar disorder (BD). However, no study has investigated whether EI mediates the relationship between CM and PSF in patients with BD. Here, we aimed to assess the association of CM with EI and PSF in euthymic patients with BD compared with healthy controls (HCs).

item.title: From brain networks to peripheral signatures: candidate biomarkers for major depressive disorder.
item.description: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading cause of disability worldwide, yet its neural basis and biomarkers remain elusive. In this study, we combined neuroimaging, transcriptomics, proteomics, and machine learning to bridge large-scale brain network dysfunction with peripheral molecular signatures. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) from 544 MDD patients and 569 healthy controls (HC) revealed altered network topology involving thalamic, fronto-striatal, and parietal regions.

item.title: Psychiatric comorbidities in pediatric epilepsy: a single-center retrospective study highlighting the burden of depressive symptoms.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: Epilepsy in the pediatric population is frequently associated with psychiatric comorbidities. Depression is of particular clinical significance given its elevated incidence and substantial impact on quality of life, treatment adherence, and psychosocial functioning. The prevalence of depression in children with epilepsy ranges from 7% to 14%, considerably higher than the 1-5% reported in the general pediatric population.

item.title: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose-Involved Hospitalizations - United States, 2016-2025.
item.description: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a serious, often underrecognized complication among patients hospitalized for drug overdose. Although overdose mortality has recently declined in the United States, less is known about whether serious nonfatal complications, including AKI, have followed similar trends. Adjusted percentages of hospitalizations of patients with drug overdose and AKI were calculated using hospital discharge data during 2016-2025.

item.title: Media-based surveillance of suicide in Türkiye: a mixed-methods analysis of epidemiological patterns, homicide-suicide events, and contextual factors.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Suicide remains a major public health concern worldwide, yet official mortality statistics often provide limited information regarding the contextual circumstances surrounding suicide events. Media reports provide insights into demographic characteristics, suicide methods, homicide-suicide incidents, and the social contexts associated with these events. This study aimed to examine suicide cases reported in Turkish media using a mixed-methods approach with epidemiological surveillance and qualitative document analysis. METHODS: A convergent mixed-methods design was employed.

item.title: Ketamine Beyond Anaesthesia: Analgesic, Psychiatric, Antitumour, and Immunomodulatory Actions and Their Signalling Mechanisms.
item.description: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To synthesize current evidence on ketamine for cancer-related pain and its intersecting psychiatric, anti-tumor, and immunomodulatory actions, emphasizing mechanisms, clinical relevance, and uncertainties relevant to oncology. RECENT FINDINGS: Ketamine provides analgesia primarily through non-competitive antagonism of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors and additional effects on excitatory, inhibitory, and opioid-related signaling.

item.title: Treatment-Resistant Psychosis in an Adolescent at Risk of Metabolic Syndrome: A Case Report.
item.description: Management of treatment-resistant psychosis is inherently complex, presenting unique clinical challenges in pediatric populations when metabolic syndrome risk limits pharmacologic options. We report a case of an adolescent with rapid decline and persistent psychotic symptoms despite trials of first-line antipsychotic agents. His refractory clinical course required careful consideration of the relative benefits of other antipsychotic therapies against their potential for significant metabolic adverse effects.

item.title: Exposure to multiple metals and adolescent major depressive disorder: a case-control study in China.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Major depressive disorder (MDD) in adolescents is a common mental health problem with a complicated cause and increasing prevalence. Previous studies reported the impact of metals on adolescents with depressive symptoms, but limited evidence is available on the relationship between metals and adolescent MDD. METHODS: A total of 203 adolescents with MDD and 203 healthy controls were recruited for this case-control study. Urinary levels of 21 metals were measured using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry.

item.title: The association of anxiety, depression, developmental disabilities, and congenital heart disease in US children and adolescents.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Congenital heart disease (CHD) has been linked to the risk of mental health or some developmental disabilities, but there is limited research on the effect of CHD on children and adolescents' mental health and developmental disabilities (varying severity) in the general children and adolescents' population. METHODS: This nationally representative study included 52,846 children and adolescents aged 6-17 years who participated in the 2022-2023 National Survey of Children's Health (NSCH) in the US from July 2022 to January 2024.

item.title: An Integrative Approach for Subtyping Mental Disorders Using Multimodal Data.
item.description: Understanding the biological and behavioral heterogeneity underlying psychiatric disorders is critical for advancing precision diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. This paper addresses the scientific question of how multimodal data, which spans clinical, cognitive, and neuroimaging measures, can be integrated to identify biologically meaningful subtypes of mental disorders. We introduce Mixed INtegrative Data Subtyping (MINDS), a Bayesian hierarchical model designed to jointly analyze mixed-type data for simultaneous dimension reduction and clustering.

item.title: Chronic post-traumatic stress disorder-related behavioral traits develop in female rats exposed to repetitive low-level blast injury and are reversible with (2R,6R)-hydroxynorketamine.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: Many military Veterans who experienced blast-related injuries during military service suffer from chronic cognitive and mental health problems. Women constitute more than 15% of active-duty U. S. military personnel and are the fastest-growing population of U. S. Veterans. For more than a decade, we have studied a rat model of repetitive low-level blast exposure designed to mimic the type of blast-related exposure that is common in military settings.

item.title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Proposed Cut-Off Values of the ASRS-R for Screening ADHD in Chinese Children and Adolescents: A Case-Control Study.
item.description: Building on the prior validation of the Revised Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS-R), this case-control study aimed to derive proposed cut-off scores for screening ADHD in Chinese children and adolescents aged 8-14 years. The study included 457 children and adolescents (106 with DSM-5 diagnosed ADHD, 351 controls) from a Shenzhen hospital. Reliability (Cronbach's α = 0.929) and validity (GFI = 0.954; rs = 0.604 with SNAP-IV) were good. ROC analysis was used to determine proposed cut-offs.

item.title: Updates in the treatment of eating disorders in 2025: a year in review in Eating Disorders: The Journal of Treatment & Prevention.
item.description: A broad range of relevant and diverse studies on the treatment of eating disorders were published in Eating Disorders: The Journal of Treatment & Prevention in 2025. We review novel treatment approaches, including interventions for individuals with complex clinical presentations, integrated primary care models, brief psychological treatments, peer support, and virtually delivered interventions. We also examine clinical, psychological, family, and treatment-related factors associated with treatment outcomes and barriers and facilitators to the implementation of Family-Based Treatment.

item.title: Experiences of Suicide Prevention Interventions and Supports for Autistic Adults: Perspectives of Autistic Adults, Family Members and Clinicians.
item.description: PURPOSE: Autistic adults experience disproportionately high rates of suicidality, yet little research has examined how they experience suicide prevention supports. This study explored perspectives on suicide prevention supports from Autistic adults, family members and clinicians. METHODS: A qualitative study using reflexive thematic analysis was conducted.

item.title: Smoking cessation interventions in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
item.description: This is a protocol for a Cochrane review (intervention). The objectives are as follows: Primary objective To assess the effects of smoking cessation interventions, compared with no intervention, usual care, placebo, or alternative interventions, on sustained abstinence from smoking in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), or co-occurring ADHD and ASD. Secondary objectives To assess whether the effects of smoking cessation interventions differ between adults with ADHD, ASD, and co‑occurring ADHD and ASD.

item.title: Algae-derived bioactive components ameliorate alcoholic liver injury and underlying mechanisms.
item.description: Alcoholic liver injury (ALI) caused by chronic excessive alcohol consumption has become a global public health issue. Current clinical interventions including abstinence, pharmacotherapy, and liver transplantation, present substantial limitations. Natural products have emerged as a research hotspot for the prevention and treatment of ALI due to their high safety and multi-target regulatory advantages. Among them, algae-derived bioactive substances have attracted considerable attention for their hepatoprotective effects.

item.title: Age-specific profiles of suicide warning signs among Korean suicide decedents, 2013-2020.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: Suicide warning signs may provide important opportunities for early recognition and intervention, yet their presentation may vary across the life course. However, population-level evidence on age-specific patterns of suicide warning signs remains limited. This study examined age-group differences in the presence and types of suicide warning signs among suicide decedents in South Korea. METHODS: We analyzed data from the Korean National Investigations of Suicide Deaths Through Police Records, 2013-2020.

item.title: What happens after being not-on-track? Patterns of change, profiles and prediction of at-risk patients.
item.description: OBJECTIVES: Clinicians often struggle to accurately identify patients at risk of treatment failure. Feedback-informed treatment offers real-time outcome monitoring to help detect and address potential treatment failures early. This study examined patterns of change among not-on-track (NOT) patients during feedback-informed treatment, explored how patients' characteristics related to these patterns, and assessed the feasibility of predicting them. METHOD: Data from 573 NOT patients in a university outpatient psychotherapy clinic were analyzed.

item.title: Acceptability of blinded continuous glucose monitoring for people with serious mental illness and type 2 diabetes: findings from an exploratory mixed-methods study.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: People with serious mental illness (SMI) experience a disproportionately high prevalence of type 2 diabetes and a reduced life expectancy of 15 to 20 years. While continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has revolutionised diabetes self-management in the general population, its feasibility and acceptability among individuals living with co-existing SMI remain largely unexamined. METHODS: The study was embedded within the DIAMONDS feasibility study.

item.title: Prenatal exposure to maternal stress hormones and the risk of autism: a neuroendocrine-epigenetic scoping review.
item.description: Maternal psychosocial stress during pregnancy is increasingly recognized as a factor capable of shaping fetal neurodevelopment through alterations in the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and placental regulatory systems. When maternal stress hormones, particularly cortisol, rise persistently during gestation, they may exceed the buffering capacity of the placenta, influencing fetal brain pathways implicated in social communication, sensory processing, and emotional regulation.

item.title: Accelerated brain aging associated with executive deficits in adolescence and early adulthood among individuals with schizophrenia and genetic high risk.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: Abnormal brain development and cognitive function are present in adolescence and early adulthood of schizophrenia (SZ). However, it is still unclear whether these developmental abnormalities and cognitive deficits occur in adolescence and early adulthood in individuals at genetic high risk (GHR). This study aims to examine brain age gap differences during adolescence and early adulthood in individuals with SZ, GHR, and healthy control (HC), as well as their associations with cognitive function.

item.title: Current situation and influencing factors of knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors related to depression among parents of adolescents with depression.
item.description: OBJECTIVE: To assess depression-related knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) among parents of adolescents hospitalized with depression and to identify associated factors. METHODS: Using purposive sampling, we surveyed 138 parents of adolescents with depression hospitalized at our center (December 2023-September 2024). Participants completed a 25-item questionnaire covering knowledge (10 items), attitudes (9 items), and practices (6 items).

item.title: Imagination and Its Disorders in Mental State Examination.
item.description: Imagination is part of ordinary psychic life, but, in somewhat distorted forms, also an aspect of different key psychopathological concepts and hence of immediate clinical importance. In this review, we present principal findings from clinical psychopathological research examining basic disturbances of imagination in the schizophrenia spectrum, obsessive symptoms, and related phenomena in other mental disorders, including the suggested DSM-6 category of maladaptive daydreaming.

item.title: Delusions: Concept, Structure, and Clinical Boundaries.
item.description: Delusions are traditionally defined as false, incorrigible beliefs that are held with certainty. This article revisits classical phenomenological accounts of delusion, particularly those of Karl Jaspers and Kurt Schneider, and argues that delusions are better understood through their structural rather than purely content-based features.

item.title: Formal Thought Disorders.
item.description: Formal thought disorder (FTD), changes in the form (as opposed to the content) of thinking, has a largely unknown pathophysiological basis or bases, although language, frontal/executive, and semantic memory mechanisms have been implicated. FTD is a major symptom of schizophrenia and is also common in mania, with there being a marked overlap of clinical features between the 2 disorders.

item.title: Disorder of Basic Selfhood in the Schizophrenia Spectrum: A Novel Phenotype.
item.description: This article conceptualizes schizophrenia as a disorder of subjectivity centered on disturbances of basic self. Drawing on phenomenological resources, clinical work and clinical research, it argues that anomalous self-experiences is a core and defining feature of the schizophrenia spectrum. Using the Examination of Anomalous Self-Experience, the article demonstrates how disruptions in core aspects of selfhood such as the sense of self-presence, embodiment, and self-world demarcation, generate characteristic clinical phenomena.
